title: Stefan-Boltzmann Radiant Exitance

M.description: Radiant exitance (power emitted per unit area)

applicability: Governs the total IR radiation measured by the thermal camera. Emissivity errors directly affect temperature measurement: 5% emissivity error ≈ 2–3°C temperature error at ambient temperatures. Critical to use correct emissivity for the surface material.

title: Thermal Contrast — Seepage Detection Threshold

ΔT.description: Temperature difference between seepage zone and surrounding surface

T_background.description: Ambient surface temperature of dry ground

NETD.description: Noise Equivalent Temperature Difference of camera

applicability: For camera with NETD = 0.05°C and SNR = 5: minimum detectable ΔT ≈ 0.25°C. Practical minimum considering environmental noise (wind, clouds): ΔT ≥ 0.5–1.0°C for reliable field detection.

title: Ground Resolution — Thermal Camera from UAS
applicability: Example: 12 μm pixel, 13 mm lens, 30 m altitude → GSD = (12e-6 × 30)/0.013 = 0.028 m = 28 mm/pixel. Much coarser than RGB GSD from same altitude. Seepage zone must span multiple thermal pixels for reliable detection — minimum detectable feature ≈ 3–5 × GSD_thermal.

title: Groundwater Temperature Approximation

MAAT.description: Mean annual air temperature at the site

G.description: Geothermal gradient (typically 25–30°C/km in stable continental crust)

applicability: For shallow seepage through dams/levees (d < 50 m), geothermal contribution is negligible (< 1.5°C). T_gw ≈ MAAT ± 2°C. Seasonal variation dampens with depth: at ~10 m depth, temperature is essentially constant year-round. This constant temperature creates the contrast used for detection.
source: Anderson (2005) Heat as a Ground Water Tracer

title: Seepage Velocity from Temperature Profile (Heat Tracer)

κ.description: Thermal diffusivity of saturated soil (≈ 0.5–1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s)

ΔT_up.description: Temperature amplitude at upper measurement point

ΔT_down.description: Temperature amplitude at lower measurement point

applicability: Quantitative seepage estimation using distributed temperature sensing (DTS) or point temperature loggers. More commonly done with fiber-optic DTS cables buried along levee/dam toes. Surface thermal IR provides qualitative detection; subsurface temperature profiling provides quantitative flow estimation.

title: Evaporative Cooling Effect
applicability: In warm, dry conditions, seepage zones may appear cooler than surrounding dry surfaces due to evaporative cooling (opposite of the warm-in-winter signal). This dual behavior means seepage may appear warm or cool depending on season and conditions — interpretation requires understanding of the thermal regime.

title: Fiber-Optic DTS Temperature Resolution

δT_base.description: Base temperature resolution at reference conditions (0.01–0.1°C)

applicability: DTS measures temperature continuously along fiber-optic cables (up to 30 km length). Typical resolution: 0.1°C at 1 m spatial, 60 s integration. Used for continuous seepage monitoring in dam/levee toes. Raman-based (temperature only) or Brillouin-based (temperature + strain).
source: Selker et al. (2006), Henault et al. (2010)

title: Minimum Seepage Flow for Thermal Detection

Q_min.description: Minimum seepage flow rate detectable at one thermal pixel

A_pixel.description: Area of one thermal pixel on the ground

ΔT_seepage.description: Temperature difference between seepage water and ground

applicability: Order-of-magnitude estimate. Detection depends heavily on seepage concentration (focused flow more detectable than diffuse), surface conditions, and thermal pixel size. Very diffuse seepage (< 10⁻⁷ m/s Darcy velocity) may not produce detectable surface anomalies.
